first.rationale: Two of the three current problems are funnel-mechanics problems (onboarding completion -4%, activation -6%), and only one is competitive pricing. Shortening onboarding (memory_86) is the single lever that plausibly addresses both funnel declines at once and compounds into qualified revenue, whereas promotional pricing (memory_73) buys acquisition volume at the cost of price anchoring, margin, and likely lower-quality accounts — the exact opposite of the 'sustainable long-term qualified revenue' objective, and the most tempting reflex given the competitor headline. I am verifying memory_86 because it is the memory I intend to act on and I need its original record: 'improved completion rates' may have been measured on completion itself rather than on retained or monetized accounts, and it was scoped to self-serve, which may not generalize. I am verifying memory_31 because signup simplification carries a specific downstream value risk that consolidation tends to erase: cutting required fields lifts first-week activation while degrading lead qualification data, which shows up later as worse routing, worse sales-assist conversion (memory_44), and weaker qualified pipeline — a local win that is a global loss. I am verifying memory_73 not because I intend to use it but because it is the strongest competing pull this week and I want to know whether 'strong acquisition and revenue lift' was gross revenue over a short window with no retention or discount-expiry cohort followed. I am not verifying memory_91 or memory_57: activation messaging is a reasonable second choice but is a narrower lever than onboarding, and referral incentives depend on an established-customer base that does not address either declining metric. These memories are consolidated summaries, not raw results; each states an effect without the horizon, population, or guardrail metrics it was measured against, so I am treating them as directional priors rather than settled facts. If the memory_86 record shows the effect was measured only on completion rate, or only in a self-serve cohort unlike the currently declining one, I will downgrade to a small guarded test or switch to activation_messaging. I will instrument this as a standard experiment with explicit downstream guardrails — 30/60-day retention, conversion to paid, and qualified-pipeline quality — rather than declaring victory on completion rate, because completion is the proxy and qualified revenue is the thing.

final.rationale: Verification largely confirmed the onboarding prior and disqualified the tempting one. exp_86 is the only candidate whose original record shows a downstream guardrail moving the right way: completion +13% and time-to-value -2.1 days were accompanied by 30-day retention +3%, so the lift was not purchased by pulling unqualified accounts through the funnel. It also targets both currently declining metrics — onboarding completion -4% and, via faster time-to-value, activation -6% — which is the strongest fit of any single lever to the actual diagnosis. exp_73 is now explicitly ruled out rather than merely suspected: the consolidated memory said 'strong acquisition and revenue lift' and silently dropped 30-day retention -12% and the source author's own instruction not to generalize targeted discounting. That cohort does not survive first renewal, so promotional pricing would buy signup volume this quarter and destroy qualified revenue next one — precisely the failure the primary objective is written against. The competitor's pricing move is real, but matching it with a discount is answering a durable positioning problem with a lever that is documented to decay. exp_31 is instructive but not chosen: it is a genuine effect (+4% qualified revenue) yet it carries retention -1%, is confirmed only on SMB and explicitly not replicated elsewhere, and it works by removing signup fields — which degrades the qualification data that the sales-assisted enterprise path depends on. I am deliberately not stacking it with onboarding this week; the slot is one experiment and confounding two funnel changes would leave me unable to attribute either. Residual uncertainty I am carrying rather than resolving: exp_86's retention read stops at 30 days, so a +3% figure there is not evidence of renewal-cycle durability, and the original was run on self-serve accounts which may not match the cohort driving the current decline. Accordingly I will run this as a standard experiment with holdout, and judge it on 30- and 60-day retention, conversion to paid, and qualified-pipeline quality — not on completion rate, which is the proxy that exp_73 shows can move hard in the wrong direction. If retention or paid conversion degrades in the holdout comparison, I stop rather than scale, and activation_messaging (memory_91, still unverified and treated as directional only) becomes the next candidate.
